name: Relations with Neighboring Countries
description: Iran’s relations with nearby countries connect diplomatic negotiations with border security, energy exchange, transport, and migration. Documented cooperation mechanisms coexist with serious security disputes and humanitarian pressures.

seo.title: Iran and Its Neighbors: Diplomacy, Borders and Cooperation
seo.description: Explore Iran’s regional relationships through diplomatic agreements, border security, energy links, migration, and the limits of cooperation.

content.heading: Several relationships, rather than one regional policy
content.content:
Iran’s neighborhood is best understood through specific relationships and practical issues. The sources examined here document diplomatic reconciliation with Saudi Arabia, regular consultation with Türkiye, security negotiations with Pakistan, economic cooperation with Armenia, and humanitarian pressures involving Afghanistan. Together, they show why a diplomatic meeting, an operating infrastructure link, and a statement of future intentions require different interpretations. None alone establishes that a relationship is consistently cooperative. [s1][s3][s4][s5][s6]

This account covers selected relationships. It does not establish a complete assessment of every neighboring state or the operational condition of borders and transport routes at the research cutoff.

content.heading: Saudi Arabia: restoring diplomatic channels
content.content:
The March 2023 Beijing agreement committed Iran and Saudi Arabia to resume diplomatic relations and reopen their missions. Its language emphasized sovereignty and non-interference. The statement also acknowledged earlier dialogue hosted by Iraq and Oman, placing China’s role within a longer regional process. A subsequent trilateral meeting in December reported that the embassies had reopened. [s1][s2]

These documents establish an agreement and a reported implementation milestone. They do not demonstrate resolution of every regional disagreement. That distinction became especially important during the 2026 war: SIPRI, an independent peace and security research institute, described Iranian attacks affecting Gulf Arab states. Earlier reconciliation cannot therefore be presented as proof of continuing regional stability. [s7]

content.heading: Türkiye and Pakistan: mechanisms for managing differences
content.content:
Türkiye’s foreign ministry identifies the High Level Cooperation Council, established in 2014, as a structural basis for relations with Iran. Its chronology records recurring leadership meetings and later ministerial contacts. This is evidence of an established consultation mechanism; the number of meetings or agreements does not measure how effectively disagreements were resolved. [s3]

Pakistan illustrates the coexistence of confrontation and diplomatic repair. Associated Press reported that the neighbors exchanged cross-border strikes in January 2024. During an Iranian presidential visit that April, they pledged closer security cooperation. Such commitments describe an intended response to insecurity, rather than independently verified success in preventing further attacks. [s4]

content.heading: Armenia: infrastructure and economic connections
content.content: Armenia’s foreign ministry describes cooperation with Iran in energy, transport, environmental protection, education, and culture. Its account identifies a cross-border bridge, a gas-for-electricity arrangement, and existing power transmission lines among implemented projects, while distinguishing another transmission line as under construction. This distinction matters: an announced connection should not be counted as operating capacity. The same source records an intergovernmental committee and diplomatic representation, showing that the relationship extends beyond individual infrastructure projects. These are Armenia’s official descriptions; this research did not independently audit their operating performance. [s5]

content.heading: Afghanistan: diplomacy with direct human consequences
content.content:
Movement across Iran’s eastern border also connects regional policy with household security. In May 2026, the United Nations and humanitarian partners launched a response plan for Afghans returning from Iran and Pakistan. It linked assistance at border crossings with support in receiving communities. The plan’s future return figures were projections, not completed movements. [s6]

For readers, the useful distinction is between diplomatic arrangements and their consequences for people: access to shelter, services, livelihoods, and protection. Assessing the relationship requires both perspectives. This page’s evidence does not establish final return totals or humanitarian outcomes through October 2026. [s6]

name: Relations with China
description: Iran and China established a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2016 and signed a long-term cooperation plan in 2021. Their relationship combines diplomatic coordination and proposed economic cooperation, but the framework itself does not establish specific investment commitments or completed projects.

seo.title: Iran–China Relations: Partnership, Cooperation and Its Limits
seo.description: Understand Iran and China’s strategic partnership, the long-term cooperation plan, and the distinction between diplomatic commitments and implementation.

content.heading: What the partnership establishes
content.content:
The modern framework examined here began with the comprehensive strategic partnership announced during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Iran in January 2016. According to China’s ambassador to Iran, the two governments then envisaged a long-term cooperation agreement drawing on economic complementarity and existing work in energy, infrastructure, industry, and technology. [s1]

A strategic partnership is a diplomatic framework. Its title alone does not establish how much money has been invested, which projects are operating, or whether either government has accepted a mutual defense obligation. Those questions require examination of specific agreements and implementation evidence. This distinction is particularly useful when reading expansive descriptions of the relationship. [s1][s2]

content.heading: The long-term plan and the investment claims
content.content:
Foreign ministers Wang Yi and Mohammad Javad Zarif signed the cooperation plan in March 2021. In a subsequent public interview, China’s ambassador described it as a framework for future economic and cultural cooperation, without quantified contracts or specific targets. It should therefore not be presented as an already financed investment program. [s1]

An independent examination by Al Sharq Strategic Research likewise distinguished the document’s aspirations from contractual commitments. Its analysis challenged widely circulated claims that the plan guaranteed a vast, predetermined investment package. The important editorial question is not whether cooperation was discussed, but whether a particular investment has a documented contract, financing, implementation timetable, and demonstrated outcome. The sources inspected here do not establish an aggregate value for completed investment under the plan. [s2]

content.heading: A diplomatic role extending beyond bilateral ties
content.content:
China’s hosting of the March 2023 Iran–Saudi Arabia talks illustrates a regional dimension of the relationship. The resulting joint statement committed the two regional states to restore diplomatic relations and acknowledged earlier negotiations hosted by Iraq and Oman. China’s role therefore built on an existing process rather than beginning it from nothing. [s3]

The December follow-up statement reported the reopening of embassies and continuing trilateral consultation. That is a concrete diplomatic milestone, but it is narrower than a settlement of all disputes. For Iran, the episode demonstrates that relations with Beijing can involve negotiations with other governments as well as bilateral projects. The documents do not establish that China assumed responsibility for regional security. [s3][s4]

content.heading: Support expressed through official diplomacy
content.content:
At a July 2025 meeting in Tianjin, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi expressed support for Iran’s sovereignty and for defending its interests through political negotiation. The Chinese account also recorded Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s commitment to closer relations and exchanges. These statements document diplomatic positions and intentions, rather than a measurable economic result. [s5]

A useful assessment keeps three questions separate: what the governments announce, what they formally agree, and what they implement. The inspected record supports a continuing diplomatic framework and identifiable meetings. It does not, by itself, support claims of unlimited Chinese backing or demonstrate delivery of the plan’s broader economic aspirations. Developments after July 2025 require further research before this account can serve as a complete contemporary assessment. [s1][s2][s5]

content.title: Selected documented stages of the relationship
content.content:
```mermaid
timeline
  title Selected Iran-China diplomatic milestones
  2016 : Comprehensive strategic partnership announced
  2021 : Long-term cooperation plan signed
  2023 : China hosts Iran-Saudi talks
  2023 : Trilateral follow-up reports reopened embassies
  2025 : Foreign ministers meet in Tianjin
```
content.summary: These milestones describe diplomatic frameworks and meetings. They do not measure investment delivery or establish a defense alliance.

name: Relations with Russia
description: Iran and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in January 2025 covering security and broader cooperation. Their relationship also involves arms transfers, economic arrangements, and transport initiatives, whose implementation must be assessed separately from treaty language.

seo.title: Iran–Russia Relations: Treaty, Security and Economic Cooperation
seo.description: Examine the Iran–Russia strategic treaty, documented security ties, Eurasian trade arrangements, and the distinction between commitments and results.

content.heading: A broad framework for cooperation
content.content:
Iran and Russia signed their comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in January 2025. The published text calls for expanded cooperation across fields of mutual interest, including security and defense. Its breadth matters: the relationship cannot be understood solely through military exchanges, even though those exchanges have attracted substantial international attention. [s1]

Reuters’ examination identified provisions concerning energy investment, peaceful nuclear projects, and financial cooperation alongside security commitments. These provisions establish intended directions of cooperation. They do not establish that every proposed power station, payment mechanism, or energy project has been financed or completed. Assessing implementation requires evidence beyond the signing ceremony and the treaty’s stated ambitions. [s2]

content.heading: What the security language actually requires
content.content:
The treaty’s response to aggression is narrower than an automatic promise to enter a war. Article 3 states that, if one party faces aggression, the other must not provide assistance to the aggressor that would sustain it, and must help seek a settlement under the United Nations Charter and applicable international law. That wording should not be replaced with a claim that the treaty requires immediate military intervention. [s1]

Reuters also identifies joint exercises, intelligence cooperation, and military-technical cooperation among the agreement’s provisions. Such commitments create channels for activity but do not reveal the volume, timing, or effectiveness of every exchange. The practical significance of the partnership therefore depends on both its legal wording and independently documented conduct. [s2]

content.heading: Arms cooperation and the war in Ukraine
content.content:
Independent research places arms transfers at the center of the relationship’s recent security dimension. SIPRI’s 2026 assessment describes Iran as a supplier of drones and missiles used by Russia in Ukraine after the full-scale invasion began in 2022. These findings concern documented wartime cooperation, rather than merely the treaty’s prospective language. [s3]

The same assessment observes that Russian-supplied aircraft and air defenses appeared to provide limited protection during Israeli and United States attacks on Iran. Its cautious wording matters: possession of imported equipment is different from demonstrated battlefield effectiveness. Neither arms sales nor a strategic partnership title should be treated as a complete measure of the protection one state provides another. [s3]

content.heading: Trade arrangements and unfinished practical work
content.content:
Economic cooperation also operates through the Eurasian Economic Union, a regional grouping that includes Russia. In October 2026, Interfax reported discussions between the union’s economic commission and Iranian officials about implementing their free trade agreement, which entered into force in May 2025. The talks addressed transport costs, border procedures, market access, and electronic customs cooperation. [s4]

The North–South international transport corridor is part of this agenda. Yet discussions about reducing costs and developing procedures are evidence of ongoing work, not proof that every route or administrative system is complete. Furthermore, union-wide trade figures cannot be silently relabeled as Russian–Iranian bilateral trade. The report describes a regional arrangement involving several economies. [s4]

A careful reading therefore separates treaty obligations, observed military cooperation, and commercial implementation. Each reveals a different part of the relationship; none substitutes for a complete assessment of developments through the research cutoff. [s1][s3][s4]

content.title: Different instruments, different kinds of evidence
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Iran-Russia partnership treaty"] -->|"Sets security commitments"| B["Security cooperation"]
  A -->|"Provides a framework for"| C["Energy and financial cooperation"]
  D["Eurasian Economic Union-Iran trade agreement"] -->|"Provides separate trade rules"| E["Regional goods trade"]
  E -->|"Implementation talks address"| F["Border procedures and transport costs"]
```
content.summary: The bilateral treaty and the regional trade agreement are distinct instruments. Their provisions and implementation discussions do not establish that all associated projects or systems are complete.
